          What Did We Learn From Jürgen Klopp’s First Game Back in Management?
        
      
                          
                      Sep 25, 2026
          
                      David Segar / Author
                  
      
              
                      
                  
          

    
              
      
              
                    
After over two years away from the dugout, Jürgen Klopp returned to the touchline on Thursday as Germany boss. How did it go, and were there signs that he can revive Die Nationalelf?
For a long time, Jürgen Klopp insisted he may never return to football management.

The 59-year-old left Liverpool in May 2024 after admitting he was “running out of energy” following nine years at Anfield. After a break from the game altogether, he returned with Red Bull as its head of global soccer, overseeing the running of their various teams around the world.
The managerial bug can be infectious, though, and following Germany’s disappointing 2026 World Cup and the departure of Julian Nagelsmann, Klopp was asked to come to the rescue.
On Thursday, he took charge of his first game since May 2024 as Germany travelled to face old rivals the Netherlands in their 2026-27 UEFA Nations League opener.

Expectations were high. Klopp leading the German national team always felt like it would happen eventually, and there is optimism the former Mainz and Borussia Dortmund boss can have the same revolutionary impact he had at all three clubs he’s managed.

As mentioned, Germany had a poor World Cup this summer. They started by thrashing Curaçao 7-1, though they needed a late winner to overcome Ivory Coast after that, before losing 2-1 to Ecuador in their final group game.
That was not ideal preparation for a tough last-32 clash with Paraguay, and so it proved. Germany struggled with their opponents’ physical approach and were ultimately eliminated on penalties.
Klopp signed a four-year deal to take over from Nagelsmann, overseeing the Euro 2028 and 2030 World Cup campaigns. His primary challenge is the Nations League, though, and it was a big test first up.

Not only was he taking on the Netherlands in Amsterdam, complete with their own new gaffer in Xavi Hernández – also managing his first game since May 2024 after leaving Barcelona – but he was set to face three of his former Liverpool players. Virgil van Dijk, Ryan Gravenberch and Cody Gakpo all started for the Dutch, and one of them went on to deny his old boss a debut victory.

Klopp took the unusual step of naming a 44-man squad, with Augsburg goalkeeper Finn Dahmen the only player set to be present for all four Nations League games in this international window. One group of players will be available for the first two (vs Netherlands and Greece) and then others will join up for the last two (vs Serbia and Greece).

The move was met with general approval in Germany, allowing Klopp to look at many players, introduce new and exciting faces, and also protect players from too much football across the elongated international break.

That doesn’t entirely eradicate the risk of injury, though, and that was apparent when Jamal Musiala pulled up in the warm-up in Amsterdam. On top of that, Kai Havertz could only play the first half hour after being on the receiving end of a nasty challenge by Quinten Timber, the brother of Havertz’s Arsenal teammate Jurriën.

An early scare came from one of Klopp’s former charges, with Van Dijk converting a Tijjani Reijnders corner, only for the goal to be ruled out after a VAR check judged Brian Brobbey to have fouled Marc-André ter Stegen.
There was some familiarity in the first XI Klopp named as Germany manager. Joshua Kimmich was handed his 115th cap, taking him past Toni Kroos (114) and into seventh place outright.

There was also a new face in the side, with Freiburg right-back Philipp Treu earning his first cap, and he played a key role in the first goal of the Klopp era. Treu’s low cross into the Dutch box from the right was blocked by the sliding Jan Paul van Hecke, but the loose ball fell kindly for Felix Nmecha, who finished calmly. It was somewhat appropriate that a Dortmund player scored the first goal under Klopp, given the outstanding success he had with BVB between 2008 and 2015.

It wasn’t without some controversy. Brobbey was down hurt on the turf at the time and Germany played on while Dutch players were imploring them to kick it out. Ultimately, it was at the referee’s discretion and despite some disagreements between Denzel Dumfries and Kimmich, Klopp’s side were well within their rights to play on, and it was 1-0.

It was familiar shape from Klopp’s side. Havertz was the striker but dropped deep – indeed, Nadiem Amiri had a more advanced average position in the first 30 minutes – while the two full-backs got forward with regularity. The wide forwards, Karim Adeyemi and Kevin Schade, were the two most-advanced German players in that first half hour before Havertz was forced off.

Another new face, Younes Ebnoutalib, replaced Havertz, and if anything, Germany looked even better with the Eintracht Frankfurt man up top. It wasn’t entirely polished but there was energy, there was effort, and there was counter pressing so synonymous with Klopp.
After the game, Treu told RTL: “We wanted to press them from the front, put them under pressure, be difficult to play against and play with intensity.
